newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronaut set for four months in space.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronaut set for four months in space.

text.p: Shuttle Atlantis will depart space station Mir on Monday, leaving astronaut John Blaha behind for four months with two Russian crewmates he never expected to work with.

Blaha had trained for six months at Star City, outside Moscow, with cosmonauts Gennadi Manakov and Pavel Vinogradov. But just days before the two Russians were due to head for Mir in a Soyuz spacecraft, they were grounded for medical reasons.
Manakov had failed a routine heart checkup, and Russian flight rules required that both men be replaced with their backups.
Blaha, a 54-year-old Vietnam veteran with four shuttle missions to his credit, was devastated when NASA called to tell him the news.

"I knew I was going to go, but I thought it was terrible," he told Reuters before his launch last Monday. "I got to Star City in Russia. I wasn't happy. I went to a breakfast on Monday where they send the crew off. It was terrible, absolutely terrible. I wasn't in a happy mood at all."

This wasn't the first time Blaha had faced a change of crew. For a year he prepared to fly with cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin, but in February they were assigned to another mission.
As for his new crewmates, Valeri Korzun and Alexander "Sasha" Kaleri, they were almost strangers.
A few days after hearing the "jolting" news, Blaha spent some time with Korzun and Kaleri as they prepared for launch at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

"I decided we have got to start getting happy," Blaha said. "I think it's going to work. They're both good people. They want it to work and I do. The only way to be happy is to try to be nice with each other."
On Sunday Blaha appeared on television shoulder to shoulder with Korzun and said he was comfortable in his new home after just three days aboard the Russian orbital outpost.
"Valeri and Sasha ... have really helped me out in the last few days," he said. "I had a great night's sleep, and I feel very good on the Mir right now."

Blaha, who replaces space marathon woman Shannon Lucid, will bid farewell to the shuttle crew early on Monday when the hatches close between the craft. He will be left with his Russian colleagues until Atlantis returns in January to pick him up.

If Blaha doesn't get on with his crewmates, he can always retire to one of Mir's interconnected modules and watch a movie. Among the 50 videotapes he took to Mir are the "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" movies.
